strengths: Well-motivated systematic probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that clearly isolates and demonstrates a specific weakness of LLM world models: degradation in long-horizon procedural alignment despite strong short-horizon prediction.

The proposed R-WoM framework is a clean, practically motivated combination of reasoning-based RAG (query rewriting + LLM reranking), single-pass LongCoT rollout (vs. costly iterative rollout), and listwise (relative) reward estimation instead of absolute scoring.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across two realistic and challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena) and three different backbone LLMs (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet), showing consistent gains over Vanilla, RAG, and WoM baselines.

Thoughtful ablations addressing RQ2 (oracle vs retrieved vs no grounding) and RQ3 (performance vs imagination horizon), which directly support the paper's central claim that grounding helps stabilize long-horizon rollouts.

Detailed appendix with prompts, tutorial sources, domain-level breakdowns, retrieval ablations (query rewriting/reranking), and a careful cost/efficiency analysis comparing to iterative rollout (WebDreamer), improving transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The probing tasks use relatively small sample sizes (100, 40, and 98 examples respectively split across two benchmarks and three models), limiting the statistical robustness of the preliminary analysis that motivates the whole paper.

The full-procedure planning alignment task is judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet, which is also one of the models being evaluated on this task, raising concerns about self-evaluation bias in the probing results.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: retrieval-augmented grounding, LLM reranking, and listwise (relative) reward/ranking are all well-established ideas individually; the main contribution is their combination for world-model rollouts rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

End-to-end absolute success rates remain modest (roughly 26-41% on OSWorld and 22-35% on WebArena even with R-WoM), and some baseline comparisons (e.g., Claude-3.5 Vanilla vs RAG on OSWorld) have overlapping error bars, making certain individual improvements less convincing.

Experiments are restricted to curated task subsets where tutorials are available and where the authors themselves manually annotated 'oracle' reference chunks, which were also used to build/evaluate retrieval and full-procedure alignment; this manual curation could introduce selection bias and limits generalizability to the full benchmarks or tutorial-scarce domains (acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically explored).

The WoM baseline is the authors' own reimplementation of WebDreamer using LongCoT rather than the original iterative approach, and other recent world-model baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., WKM, WebEvolver) are not included in the end-to-end comparison, weakening the completeness of the baseline comparison.

No formal ablation isolating the individual contribution of listwise reward estimation versus absolute reward within the R-WoM framework itself (the comparison is only indirect via WoM vs R-WoM, which differs in grounding as well).

strengths: Systematic and well-designed probing study (next-state identification, full-procedure planning alignment, milestone transition recognition) that clearly demonstrates a specific failure mode of LLM world models — degradation over long-horizon planning despite strong short-horizon prediction — providing good motivation for the proposed method.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three backbone models (Qwen-2.5-VL-72B, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet, plus extended results with Claude-4/4.5-Sonnet) and two realistic, challenging benchmarks (OSWorld, WebArena), with consistent gains over Vanilla, RAG, and WebDreamer baselines.

Extensive ablations covering retrieval component quality (query rewriting + reranking, recall@k), grounding quality (ungrounded vs retrieved vs oracle tutorials), imagination horizon sensitivity, listwise vs absolute reward design, candidate size, and judge robustness (cross-judge consistency), which strengthens the credibility of the design choices.

Thoughtful engineering for efficiency (adaptive action branching, deduplication, LongCoT single-pass rollout instead of iterative rollouts) with a clear cost-performance tradeoff analysis (token usage, latency, WM trigger reduction) which improves practical applicability.

Addresses a realistic and understudied problem: knowledge scarcity and grounding for world models in complex, realistic computer-use environments (as opposed to text-based or video-only settings), including a tutorial-scarce extension via self-play synthesis.
Detailed appendix with prompts, dataset/tutorial source details, and reproducibility information.
weaknesses: Evaluation subsets are quite small (e.g., 100/40/98 samples for probing tasks; 87/361 OSWorld and 113/301 WebArena tasks for main experiments), and the main experiments are restricted to the subset of tasks with tutorial coverage, which may bias results in favor of R-WoM and limits generalizability claims to the full benchmark distributions.

The core technical contribution is a fairly incremental combination of established techniques (RAG with query rewriting/reranking, LongCoT rollout, listwise reward ranking) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty over prior tutorial-augmented agent works (AgentTrek, TongUI, Learn-by-Interact) and world-model works (WebDreamer, WMA, WebEvolver) is mainly in combining them for inference-time grounding.

Reported relative improvements vary widely across models and benchmarks (5.6%–23.4%) without deeper analysis explaining this variance, making it hard to assess how robust/predictable the method's benefit is.

The full-procedure planning alignment judgment relies on an LLM judge (Claude-3.7-Sonnet by default) checked against only two other judges on a small sample, which may not fully rule out judge bias, especially since the same model family is both policy/world model and (in some cases) evaluator.

No direct comparison against other recent world-model baselines explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., WKM, WebEvolver) despite these being close competitors; only WebDreamer is used as the grounded/ungrounded world-model baseline.

The oracle-tutorial experiments rely on manual, human-curated tutorial annotation, which is not scalable and somewhat limits the practical takeaway about real-world retrieval-only performance ceilings.

Content-modification tasks remain a substantial failure mode (as shown in the failure analysis), suggesting the method's benefits may be concentrated in navigation/information-seeking tasks rather than the harder, more valuable modification tasks.
